subject: chemistry-1
question: Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine all appear in Group 17 of the periodic table. Which statement best explains why these three elements show similar chemical behavior?

options.text: They occupy the same period, so their valence electrons fill the same principal energy level
They have nearly equal atomic masses, so their nuclei exert similar attraction
They have equal numbers of core electrons, so the same nuclear pull reaches each outer shell
They each hold 7 valence electrons, so they gain or share electrons in similar ways

explanation:
For main-group elements the group number gives the valence electron count; Group 17 members have 17 - 10 = 7 electrons in the outermost shell. Chemical behavior is governed almost entirely by valence electrons, so all three need one additional electron to reach an octet and react in parallel ways. They sit in different periods (n = 2, 3, and 4), have very different atomic masses, and have different core electron counts (2, 10, and 28), so none of those features can explain the shared chemistry.

ELI-10: Elements in the same column of the periodic table are grouped there for a reason: they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell. Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine each have 7 outer electrons and each need just one more to reach the stable set of 8. That single shared gap is what makes them react in similar ways, even though the atoms differ greatly in size and mass. Outer electrons drive chemistry; the deeper electrons and the neutrons do not.
